Lessons.Title: Piecewise Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: interpret and graph a piecewise-defined function whose rule changes across intervals, choose the correct rule for a given input, and represent inclusive/exclusive endpoints unambiguously. This first-party Edulytics lesson is aligned to the approved local Algebra 1 Unit 4 Lesson 12 evidence and uses independently authored contexts and rules.

Original fictional food-delivery fee P(w) in dollars for a small parcel weighing w kilograms: P(w)=0. 5w when 0≤w≤5, and P(w)=3 when 5<w≤8. At 5kg the first rate gives $2. 50 (solid point), whereas just above5kg the charge jumps to $3 (open point at5 on the second piece); P(8)=$3. Above8kg is outside this service model.

This model is not an assumption that all real-world delivery services charge this way. It uses a deliberately simple break to show why a piecewise graph can include a line segment and a horizontal step, why the output at exactly the breakpoint must be specified once, and why P(5. 001) differs from P(5).

Student task: construct a table including 0,4. 9,5,5. 01,8,8. 1; draw the curve/step with labelled axes, contrast an incorrectly closed second-branch left endpoint with the correct graph, and create a second real-life step-fee function. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct cases notation, boundary tests, accurate graph and clear context/domain explanation.

First-party Cool-down (teacher-scored): Define P(x)=2x+1 for x<=3 and P(x)=5x+4 for x>3. Find P(3) and P(4), then state which endpoint at x=3 should be filled for the first piece and which should be open for the second. Numeric evaluations can be checked exactly; endpoint graphing is teacher-reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Piecewise definition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A function can use different formulas on different parts of its domain.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State each condition beside its formula.

KeyConcepts.Title: Breakpoint
KeyConcepts.Definition: Where the active rule changes, endpoint inclusion determines which value applies.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test exactly at the boundary and just above/below.

KeyConcepts.Title: Step discontinuity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Output may jump when the input crosses a boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not draw a connecting vertical segment as if it were part of a function.
KeyConcepts.Example: There are no outputs in (2.5,3) near w5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Calculate on both sides of the break
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate P(4),P(5),P(5.01),P(8).
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: At8kg second piece includes equality:3 dollars.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every input belongs to exactly one defined piece.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify open and closed endpoints
WorkedExamples.Question: How should values at w=5 appear on the graph?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: First line goes through (5,2.5) with a filled point.
Second horizontal segment at y=3 begins only for w>5.
Do not draw the vertical jump as a function segment.
WorkedExamples.Check: Only P(5)=2.5 is defined at the breakpoint.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find domain and range
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe all attainable weights and prices.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: Domain covers0≤w≤8kg by the two adjacent intervals.
First branch produces every price from0 through2.5.
WorkedExamples.Check: No input>8 is defined and no output2.75 occurs.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A function cannot give two outputs for one input.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Drawing a vertical line between step levels
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A vertical segment gives multiple outputs for the same input.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate endpoints with appropriate open/closed circles.

SummaryPoints: A piecewise function has explicit rules and interval conditions.
P(5)=2.5 while P(5.01)=3 in the example.
Teachers assess students' graphs, cases and explanations.
